steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper where a legged robot learns an egocentric visual self-model, predicting its own future state from a single onboard camera, and uses it for locomotion and for recovering after damage. Motivate why vision matters, explain self-modeling, and finish with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Vision is key to agile behavior in humans and animals
- Legged robot locomotion: proprioception traditionally, vision only for planning
- Self-modeling: separating the robot model from environment and task
- Value of self-models grows with robot and task complexity
- Our approach: egocentric visual self-model from a single RGB camera
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Vision and agile behavior

  - visually impaired people struggle without this feedback
  - not unique to humans: sighted animals more sophisticated/agile locomotion than those with limited vision (cite)

  - proprioceptive sensors (IMUs, joint encoders); vision for high-level planning

  - some multimodal work: vision + proprioception, RL policies (cite)
  - purely visual observation for locomotion unexplored -> foundation for vision in the controller, more adaptable/resilient robots
- Self-modeling
  - model-based control; decouples (deconvolves) self-model from environment/task model (cite)
  - task/environment change often, robot relatively constant
  - reuse self-model -> simpler adaptation, lifelong learning, variable tasks
  - example: tennis player learning badminton -> new rules, not running/grasping a racquet; transfer learning (cite)
- Why it matters
  - value vs model-free RL grows with robot complexity (cite) and task complexity
  - efficient accurate self-models -> practical advantage as robots get more complex
- This paper
  - purely visual data for locomotion + damage resilience; more than pose estimation
  - model own dynamics, kinematics, morphology from vision, not equations/CAD/IMU/external optical trackers (need prior knowledge/infrastructure)
  - predict future state conditioned on motor commands from frames of single RGB camera (Fig. 1)
  - uses: planner tests candidate commands before executing; damage detector compares predicted vs actual motion (visual optometry)
  - flat-ground walking not a challenge in 2024; goal = evidence for vision in walking
- Contributions
  1. locomotion from purely egocentric vision, no proprioception; network fuses frame + action sequences
  2. domain randomization + data augmentation -> zero-shot sim-to-real
  3. generalizes across robots of different morphologies/complexities
  4. recover damaged robot by re-training self-model on real-world visual data

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Human vision is very important for a lot of agile behaviors. The visual feedback we get from it is used in tasks from basic locomotion up to complex motor skills. People with visual impairments, on the other hand, often have trouble with these behaviors because they do not have this feedback. And it is not only humans who rely on vision. Many sighted animals show more sophisticated and agile locomotion than animals that have limited vision. This shows that vision is important for locomotion, and it suggests that robots, and legged robots in particular, could also benefit a lot from visual feedback.

Legged robot locomotion has traditionally used proprioceptive sensors like IMUs and joint encoders, and vision has mostly been used for high-level planning. The reason is that most visual perception systems run at a low frequency (less than 30 Hz), while stable locomotion needs high control frequencies (often more than 200 Hz). Some works have tried multimodal sensory input, where vision and proprioception are combined to train locomotion policies with reinforcement learning, but nobody has really explored what purely visual observation can do for legged robot locomotion. So looking into this could give a foundation for putting vision into the locomotion controller, and this could lead to legged robots that are more adaptable and resilient.

Self-modeling is a kind of model-based control where a model of the robot (the “self-model”) is decoupled (deconvolved) from a model of its environment and task. The main idea is that the task and environment of a robot can change a lot, but the robot itself stays relatively constant across tasks and environments. So if we separate the self-model from the model of everything else and reuse the self-model for new tasks, adaptation gets simpler in situations with lifelong learning and variable tasks.

- Why it matters
  - value vs model-free RL grows with robot complexity and task complexity
  - efficient accurate self-models -> practical advantage as robots get more complex
- This paper
  - purely visual data for locomotion + damage resilience; more than a pose estimator
  - model own dynamics, kinematics, morphology from vision instead of equations, CAD models, IMUs, external optical trackers
  - predict future state conditioned on motor commands from single RGB camera frames (Fig. 1)
  - uses: planning by testing candidate commands; damage detection by predicted vs actual motion (visual optometry)
  - flat-ground walking not a challenge in 2024; we want evidence for vision in walking
- Contributions (4): purely visual locomotion; domain randomization + augmentation for zero-shot sim-to-real; multiple robots; damage recovery by re-training

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Human vision is very important for a lot of agile behaviors. The visual feedback we get from it is used in tasks from basic locomotion up to complex motor skills. People with visual impairments, on the other hand, often have trouble with these behaviors because they do not have this feedback. And it is not only humans who rely on vision. Many sighted animals show more sophisticated and agile locomotion than animals that have limited vision. This shows that vision is important for locomotion, and it suggests that robots, and legged robots in particular, could also benefit a lot from visual feedback.

Legged robot locomotion has traditionally used proprioceptive sensors like IMUs and joint encoders, and vision has mostly been used for high-level planning. The reason is that most visual perception systems run at a low frequency (less than 30 Hz), while stable locomotion needs high control frequencies (often more than 200 Hz). Some works have tried multimodal sensory input, where vision and proprioception are combined to train locomotion policies with reinforcement learning, but nobody has really explored what purely visual observation can do for legged robot locomotion. So looking into this could give a foundation for putting vision into the locomotion controller, and this could lead to legged robots that are more adaptable and resilient.

Self-modeling is a kind of model-based control where a model of the robot (the “self-model”) is decoupled (deconvolved) from a model of its environment and task. The main idea is that the task and environment of a robot can change a lot, but the robot itself stays relatively constant across tasks and environments. So if we separate the self-model from the model of everything else and reuse the self-model for new tasks, adaptation gets simpler in situations with lifelong learning and variable tasks.

For example, a tennis player who has to learn badminton may have to learn new game rules, but they do not have to relearn how to run across a court or how to grasp a racquet, because running and grasping are common actions done by the same body. This is how self-modeling helps with transfer learning.

Also, the value of a self-model compared to model-free reinforcement learning gets bigger as the robot gets more complex and as the task gets more complex. So it is very valuable to find efficient ways to make accurate self-models, and this will be a practical advantage as robots keep getting more complex.

In this paper we look at the potential of using purely visual data in robotic systems to get locomotion and damage resilience. Our approach does more than just using vision as a pose estimator. we want robots to model their own dynamics, kinematics, and morphology from visual data, instead of using explicit equations, CAD models, and information from IMUs and external optical trackers, which need a lot of prior knowledge or infrastructure that may not exist when robots have to learn to adapt to new conditions in-situ.

We show how a robot can learn to predict its future state, conditioned on motor commands, from a sequence of frames from a single RGB camera (Fig. 1). The egocentric visual self-model we propose can be used in several ways. For example, a planning algorithm can use the model to test what happens with different candidate motor commands and then use the predictions to pick the action that is best for a task, before doing any of them in reality. Or a damage detector can use the model to compare the predicted motion with the actual motion (from visual optometry). If the predicted motion is different from the actual motion, then something must have gone wrong. We show these applications and other examples in this paper. We think this approach can be extended so robots can have more agile and adaptive behaviors.

Walking on flat ground is not a challenge anymore for a legged robot in 2024, but our work is meant to give evidence of the potential of vision in walking tasks, to help further development of more dynamic and adaptable robotic systems that integrate visual perception with robotic gait control. Our main contributions are:

1. We show a legged robot doing locomotion tasks using purely egocentric visual observations, without proprioceptive sensors. Our visual egocentric self-model network fuses sequences of high-dimensional visual observations and actions to predict future robot states

2. A domain randomization and data augmentation pipeline for robot locomotion that makes zero-shot sim-to-real transfer work.

3. We validate that our approach generalizes across multiple robots with different morphologies and complexities, which shows it could be a universal tool for diverse robotic systems.

4. We show that a damaged robot can recover its locomotion by re-training the self-model with purely visual perception data collected in the real world, which shows that our approach is adaptable and resilient when unexpected challenges happen.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Human vision plays a key role in enabling a wide range of agile behaviors. The visual feedback it provides is instrumental in tasks ranging from basic locomotion to complex motor skills [1,2,3]. In contrast, individuals with visual impairments often face challenges in performing these behaviors because this feedback is absent. This reliance on vision is not unique to humans. Many sighted animals display more sophisticated and agile locomotion patterns than their counterparts with limited visual capabilities [4,5]. This observation highlights the importance of vision in locomotion and suggests that robots, especially legged robots, could benefit significantly from visual feedback.

Traditionally, legged robot locomotion has relied on proprioceptive sensors, such as IMUs and joint encoders, with vision used mainly for high-level planning tasks. This is because most visual perception systems run at a relatively low frequency (less than 30 Hz) compared to the high control frequencies required for stable locomotion (often exceeding 200 Hz) [6,7,8]. While some works have explored multimodal sensory input, combining vision and proprioception to train locomotion policies using reinforcement learning [9,7], the potential of purely visual observation for legged robot locomotion remains unexplored. Investigating this potential could therefore provide a foundation for combining vision into the locomotion controller, leading to more adaptable and resilient legged robots.

Self-modeling is a form of model-based control that decouples (deconvolves) a model of the robot (the “self-model”) from a model of its environment and task [10,11]. The key idea is that while the task and environment of a robot may change frequently, the robot itself remains relatively constant across tasks and environments. Separating out the self-model from the model of everything else and reusing it for new tasks can therefore simplify adaptation in situations involving lifelong learning under variable tasks.

For example, if a tennis player must learn to play badminton, they may need to learn new game rules, but will not need to relearn how to run across a court or grasp a racquet, because running and grasping are common actions performed by the same body. In this way, self-modeling facilitates transfer learning [12].

Importantly, the value of a self-model compared to model-free reinforcement learning increases with the complexity of the robot [13,14] and the complexity of the task. Finding efficient ways to create accurate self-models is therefore extremely valuable and will offer a practical advantage as robot complexity continues to increase.

In this paper, we explore the potential of bringing purely visual data into robotic systems to achieve locomotion and damage resilience. Our approach goes beyond using vision merely as a pose estimator. we aim to enable robots to model their own dynamics, kinematics, and morphology from visual data instead of explicit equations, CAD models, and information from IMUs and external optical trackers, which require extensive prior knowledge or infrastructure that may not exist when robots must learn to adapt to new conditions in-situ.

Our work shows how a robot can learn to predict its future state, conditioned on motor commands, using a sequence of frames from a single RGB camera (Fig. 1). The proposed egocentric visual self-model can be used in several ways. For example, a planning algorithm can use the model to test the consequences of various candidate motor commands and use these predictions to choose the action best suited to a particular task, before executing any of them in reality. Alternatively, a damage detector can use the model to compare predicted motion to actual motion (from visual optometry). If the predicted motion deviates from the actual motion, something must have gone wrong. These applications and other examples are demonstrated in this paper. We believe this approach can be extended, allowing robots to exhibit more agile and adaptive behaviors.

Although walking on flat ground is no longer a challenge for a legged robot in 2024, our work aims to provide evidence of the potential of vision in walking tasks, in order to catalyze further development of more dynamic and adaptable robotic systems that integrate visual perception with robotic gait control. Our key contributions are as follows:

1. This work demonstrates a legged robot performing locomotion tasks using purely egocentric visual observations, without relying on proprioceptive sensors. Our visual egocentric self-model network fuses sequences of high-dimensional visual observations and actions to predict future robot states

2. A domain randomization and data augmentation pipeline for robot locomotion that enables effective zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

3. Validation of the generalizability of our approach across multiple robots with different morphologies and complexities, highlighting its potential as a universal tool for diverse robotic systems.

4. A demonstration that a damaged robot’s locomotion capabilities can be recovered by re-training the self-model on purely visual perception data collected in the real world, showing the adaptability and resilience of our approach in the face of unexpected challenges.

References:

[2] R. M. Alexander, Principles of animal locomotion . Princeton university press, 2003.
[3] D. S. Marigold and A. E. Patla, “Visual information from the lower visual field is important for walking across multi-surface terrain,” Experimental Brain Research , vol. 188, pp. 23–31, 2008.
[4] J. J. Gibson, “Visually controlled locomotion and visual orientation in animals,” British journal of psychology , vol. 49, no. 3, pp. 182–194, 1958.
[5] D. S. Marigold and A. E. Patla, “Gaze fixation patterns for negotiating complex ground terrain,” Neuroscience , vol. 144, no. 1, pp. 302–313, 2007.
